question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=x+1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{x+1}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: x real; x != -1; antiderivative on each connected interval

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=2-3x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u$, solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{2-3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-3x|+C\end{aligned}
$$
